title: How to learn world flags without mixing them up

sources.name: Italian Presidency — The Italian Tricolour Flag
Royal House of the Netherlands — Dutch flag

practice: Put your eye for detail to the test in World Flags.

sections.html: To learn world flags, pick a small set, spot one distinctive detail on each and hide the country names. Five is a friendly starting point, not a magic memory number.
sections.title: Start with five flags

sections.html:
• Layout: stripes, a cross or a plain background?
  • Colours: which ones, and in what order?
  • Symbols: what is there, and where?

The hoist is the edge attached to the pole, usually shown on the left. A photograph taken from behind can reverse the apparent order.
sections.title: Look at the design in three steps

sections.html:
Italy has equal vertical bands of green, white and red, starting at the hoist. Article 12 of its Constitution specifies the design.

Which colour is next to the flagpole?

Green. Think “green by the pole”, rather than just “red and green”.
sections.title: Try it with Italy

sections.html:
Same colours, different directions:

  • France: vertical, blue–white–red from the hoist.
  • The Netherlands: horizontal, red–white–blue from top to bottom.

The French Presidency explains the vertical distinction; the Dutch Royal House confirms the Dutch colours. Check an authoritative reference for trickier pairs: screens and lighting can alter subtle shades.
sections.title: France or the Netherlands? Same colours, different clue

sections.html:
After a round, note two flags you confused and the clue you missed. “Vertical, blue by the pole” beats “remember France”. Cover the labels and name them again before adding more.

Recognition and recall can feel surprisingly different. Ready for a shape change? Meet Nepal’s double-pennant flag.
sections.title: Keep a short list for next time

description: Learn world flags by spotting layout, colour order and symbols. Compare France with the Netherlands, then test a small set without the labels.
